interest: This report is particularly interesting as evidence of intelligence-sharing between the Soviet Union and the United States in Tokyo in mid-1940, despite the non-aggression pact between Moscow and Berlin and the prevailing mistrust of the era. It provides concrete order-of-battle details regarding the expansion of Japan's northern 'fishery patrol' into a formidable naval force of cruisers, destroyers, and submarines operating off Kamchatka and the Kuril Islands. Furthermore, the Soviet Naval Attaché's speculation regarding Japanese naval and submarine operations in the Aleutians and Alaska highlights early pre-war strategic awareness of Japanese operational interests in the North Pacific.
overview: This file consists of a two-page intelligence report (Serial No. 110 / Report No. 110-40) dated July 12, 1940, sent by the U.S. Naval Attaché in Tokyo, Lieutenant Commander H. H. Smith-Hutton, to the Director of Naval Intelligence. Drawing on information provided by the Soviet Naval Attaché in Tokyo, the report documents an unusually large concentration of Imperial Japanese Navy vessels stationed in the Kuril Islands and Kamchatka area under the guise of the annual summer 'fishery patrol.' The report outlines the force composition—including Kuma-class light cruisers, Kamikaze- and Akikaze-class destroyers, and I-53-class submarines—and notes incursions into Soviet territorial waters without incident, Soviet efforts to increase surveillance, and Russian speculation that Japanese naval craft were also operating near the Aleutian Islands and Alaska.

subfiles.about: Intelligence report on an expanded Japanese naval force operating under the guise of fishery patrol in the Kuril Islands and Kamchatka area, based on information from the Soviet Naval Attaché in Tokyo.
subfiles.from: H.H. Smith-Hutton, Lt.-Comdr., U.S. Navy, Naval Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: U.S. Naval Attaché Lt. Cmdr. H. H. Smith-Hutton reports that the Japanese Navy stationed an unusually large naval force in northern waters around the Kuril Islands and Kamchatka during the 1940 summer fishing season. According to information provided by the Soviet Naval Attaché in Tokyo, the force included two Kuma-class light cruisers, twelve Kamikaze/Akikaze-class destroyers, and eight I-53-class submarines based out of Ominato. While several Japanese vessels entered Soviet operating areas and territorial waters, they withdrew upon the approach of Soviet forces without armed incident. The report also conveys the Soviet belief that Japan was conducting training and reconnaissance, alongside suspicion of Japanese submarine activity near Alaska and the Aleutians.
